name: Carlos Blacker
bio: A gentleman of independent means, linguist and friend of Wilde's from the 1880s, who stood by him for years and to whom Wilde wrote some of the warmest letters of his exile. Fifteen survive, from 1897 to 1898. Blacker was living in Freiburg with knowledge of the Dreyfus affair; the friendship later broke over it.
bio_note: Added 2026-08-05, per Lovelle. NO CONNECTION LINE: the register is deep friendship between men and nothing read states or implies more. He is on the map because the letter below is one of the very few places where Wilde looks back over a long friendship and says what it was made of - conversation, dinners, laughter - and because he says he thought about him in prison. FIFTEEN LETTERS at repo PDF 961, 970, 971, 985, 986, 995, 1081, 1085, 1090 and others; ONE read at the page (printed 911, folio confirmed, 2026-08-05). DATES NOT RECORDED - the editors give none on the page read, and none is inferred. THE BREAK IS DOCUMENTED AFTER ALL, corrected 2026-08-06. This note previously said it was 'in the general literature and NOT documented on any page read here'. That was true of the pages then read and false as a description of the volume: the General Index lists folios 1085-8, and printed 1085 carries Wilde's own account - Blacker 'has behaved like a hypocritical ass to me', an accusation of an anonymous attack, 'I wrote him a very strong letter' - together with the Dreyfus entanglement the old note had relegated to hearsay. HOW THE ERROR WAS FOUND is worth keeping: the book's own index contradicted a claim in our data, which is exactly what indexing it was for. FOLIOS 1086-8 REMAIN UNREAD and carry, per the index, the accusation of cheating at cards and Blacker leaving his mistress to starve - Wilde's charges, not established facts, and they should be read before any of that is characterised.

context_engagements.note: Friendship, recorded without a connection line.

sources.quote: My dear old Friend, I need not tell you with what feelings of affection and gratitude I read your letter. You were always my staunch friend and stood by my side for many years. Often in prison I used to think of you: of your chivalry of nature, of your limitless generosity, of your quick intellectual sympathies, of your culture so receptive, so refined. What marvellous evenings, dear Carlos, we used to have! What brilliant dinners! What days of laughter and delight! To you, as to me, conversation - that τερπνὸν κακόν as Euripides calls it - that sweet sin of phrases - was always among the supreme aims of life, and we tired many a moon with talk, and drank many a sun to rest with wine and words. You were always the truest of friends and the most sympathetic of companions. … Many friends, such as Will Rothenstein, the artist, Conder, who is a sort of Corot of the sunlight, Ernest Dowson, the poet, and others have come to see me for a few days: and next month I hope to see Ricketts and Shannon, who decorated all my books for me, dear Robbie Ross, and perhaps some others.
sources.context: Wilde to Carlos Blacker, 12 July 1897, Chalet Bourgeat, Berneval-sur-Mer (MS Koch, Yale). Seven weeks out of prison. The elision drops a description of the chalet and the beach. τερπνὸν κακόν is Euripides' 'delightful evil'; Wilde renders it himself as 'that sweet sin of phrases'. THE ROLL-CALL AT THE END is a list of who actually came: Rothenstein, Dowson, Ricketts, Shannon and Ross are all on this map.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Wilde thought a long friendship had been made of, and who came to Berneval.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 961; printed folio 911 confirmed on the rendered page image, read 2026-08-05.

sources.quote: C. Blacker has behaved like a hypocritical ass to me, and finally wrote me a letter accusing me of having written some attack on him that appeared in some Paris paper. I need hardly say I never read the paper, or saw the attack, and that I never write anonymous attacks on people anywhere. I was so angry, I wrote him a very strong letter. He has got into a mess here through being Reinach's 'homme de paille' in his Dreyfus-Syndicat campaign and I should not wonder if he were expelled. … The comic thing about him is the moral attitude he takes up. To be either a Puritan, a prig, or a preacher is a bad thing. To be all three at once reminds one of the worst excesses of the French Revolution.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Monday, 27 June [1898], Nogent-sur-Marne (MS Clark). The elision drops the detail of Blacker's connection with Conybeare and a dismissed army officer. 'homme de paille' is a straw man or front. THIS CORRECTS THIS NODE. Its bio_note asserted until 2026-08-06 that the break with Blacker 'is NOT documented on any page read here' - a true statement about the pages then read, which the volume's own General Index contradicted by listing folios 1085-8. Reading them shows the quarrel documented in Wilde's own hand AND shows it is the Dreyfus affair, which the same note had described as merely 'in the general literature'. The editors also point to a scholarly account: J. Robert Maguire, 'Oscar Wilde and the Dreyfus Affair', Victorian Studies, Autumn 1997.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The break with Blacker, in Wilde's own words, and its entanglement with the Dreyfus affair.
